hook: LLM apps are nondeterministic — your TESTS must not be. pytest, deterministic mocking, structured logs, and automation that **refuses bad commits**.

scenes.title: pytest: tests as plain functions, power as decorators
scenes.sub: Fixtures share setup; parametrize multiplies cases

do: built, shared, torn down per test

steps.at: injected by naming it as a parameter

scenes.narration: Pytest's core bargain: write plain functions that assert, name them test-something, and the runner finds and executes them — no classes, no boilerplate, no framework ceremony. The two superpowers are fixtures and parametrize. Fixtures: setup code — a test database, a temp file, a client — written once as a decorated generator, injected by naming it as a parameter; pytest builds, shares, and tears them down per test. Parametrize: run ONE test function over a table of inputs — twenty edge cases become a single function plus a decorator, and each row reports as its own test. Test discovery, rich assertion introspection, and a plugin ecosystem come standard.

scenes.title: fixtures + parametrize in one test file
annot: The fixture is injected by NAME — no setup methods, no inheritance
Each parametrize row = an independent test in the report; one failing row doesn't hide the others
pytest.raises asserts the exception type — 'garbage in raises X' is a testable contract
scenes.narration: Notice the third parametrize row — an unanswerable question whose correct behavior is abstention. That's the GenAI testing mindset: test the CONTRACT — grounded answers, honest refusal, validation boundaries — not exact strings, because the model's phrasing varies run to run. Keep assertions structural: 'the answer contains the key fact', 'the answer cites a source', 'unknown questions are declined'. The fixture builds an in-memory vector store per test: hermetic — no shared state between tests, no test-order dependencies. If your tests pass alone and fail in the suite, shared mutable fixtures are the first suspect.

scenes.title: Mock the LLM, keep the logic: **deterministic tests**
scenes.sub: Fake the boundary, test your code

steps.at: Never call a real LLM in unit tests

do: deterministic fake at the client call

steps.at: assert your code used it correctly

scenes.narration: Never call a real LLM in unit tests: slow, costly, and nondeterministic — the same test could pass and fail with no code change. The rule: mock at the BOUNDARY — the client call — with a deterministic fake, and test everything YOUR code does around it: prompt construction, context assembly, error handling, citation formatting. unittest.mock patches the call site: patch the SDK method, return a canned response, assert your code used it correctly — right model, right parameters. Better still: define your own provider interface and inject a FakeProvider in tests — no patching, no monkey business, the same seam FastAPI taught. Either way, one suite runs offline, in milliseconds, forever deterministically.

scenes.title: FakeProvider: inject the seam, test the logic
scenes.body:
class LLMProvider(Protocol):
    async def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class FakeLLM:
    """Deterministic stand-in. Scripts EXACT replies per prompt."""
    def __init__(self, replies: dict[str, str]):
        self.replies, self.calls = replies, []

    async def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        self.calls.append(prompt)          # inspect what you sent!
        return self.replies.get(prompt, "I don't know.")

async def test_prompt_carries_context():
    fake = FakeLLM({"CTX[refund] Q: window?": "30 days"})
    rag = RagPipeline(llm=fake, store=memory_store())
    answer = await rag.ask("What is the refund window?")
    assert "30 days" in answer
    # assert on the PROMPT, not just the answer:
    assert "CTX[refund]" in fake.calls[0]      # context was assembled
    assert "citation" in fake.calls[0].lower() # citation rule included
annot: Fake records its calls → you assert on INPUTS (prompt assembly), not just outputs
The unknown-prompt default ('I don't know.') tests abstention without an LLM in the loop
Protocol-typed seam: production gets the real provider, tests get the fake — same RagPipeline code
scenes.narration: The fake doubles as an inspector: recording every prompt it receives lets you assert on what your pipeline SENDS — context assembled, citation instructions present, question included — which is where real bugs live. This is the deepest testing insight for LLM apps: your code's job is everything up to the API call; test that, deterministically, forever. What you cannot unit-test is model QUALITY — that belongs to evals, GA-20 and GA-21. Keep the boundary sharp: unit tests with fakes for logic, evals with real models for quality, and a few end-to-end smoke tests with capped spend for wiring.

scenes.title: Logs you'll actually read at 3 a.m.
scenes.sub: Structured logs, levels, and correlation IDs
scenes.narration: print debugging doesn't survive production. The logging module gives you levels — debug, info, warning, error — filtered by environment: verbose in development, info-and-above in production. Structured logging is the upgrade that matters: log JSON objects — timestamp, level, event, request-id, key fields — not prose sentences; structured logs are queryable, aggregatable, alertable, and play natively with log aggregation stacks. The request-id from FastAPI's middleware becomes your correlation ID: attach it to every log line in the request, and a user report of 'it broke' becomes a single filtered query instead of an archaeology dig. Rule: log events with context, not narration — 'retrieval returned 0 chunks, query rewritten twice' beats 'something went wrong'.

lines: log: question · rewrites · top scores · sources
NEVER: secrets · PII prompts · full responses
QueueHandler → slow sink off the loop

steps.at: logging config once at app startup

scenes.narration: The GenAI-specific logging insight: log the RETRIEVAL TELEMETRY GA-15 asked you to capture — original question, rewritten queries, top scores, chunk sources. When answer quality drops, that trail is how you diagnose which stage regressed without reproducing anything. Also: never log secrets, prompts containing PII, or full LLM responses by default — redact at the logging boundary; compliance audits ask exactly these questions. Use logging config once at app startup, and in async code remember logging is sync — one slow log sink can block the loop; queue-based handlers exist for that. Boring logging is the difference between 'we saw errors' and 'we know why'.

scenes.title: Let the toolchain **refuse** bad code before humans review it

steps.at: Ruff is the modern Python linter

scenes.narration: Manual quality discipline decays; automated discipline doesn't. Ruff is the modern Python linter — absurdly fast, one tool replacing flake8, isort, and a drawer of plugins; it catches unused imports, shadowed names, risky patterns, style violations — configurable via one pyproject file. Black is the formatter: one opinionated style, zero debates — run it and every diff shows substance, never formatting. Pre-commit wires both into git itself: a hooks file runs checks on every commit — lint, format, even pytest-fast or type checks — and REJECTS the commit if any fail. Bad code never enters history; reviewers never spend attention on style; main stays green by construction.

scenes.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml + ruff/black wired in
scenes.body:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml — checks run on EVERY git commit
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: v0.6.9
    hooks:
      - id: ruff          # lint: bugs, unused imports, style
        args: [--fix]     # auto-fix what's fixable
  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black-pre-commit-mirror
    rev: 24.10.0
    hooks:
      - id: black         # format: one style, zero debates

# pyproject.toml:
# [tool.ruff]
# line-length = 100
# select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]  # errors, pyflakes, isort,
#                                        # pyupgrade, bugbear

# pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install
# From now on: git commit runs the chain — fail = commit refused
annot: ruff --fix auto-repairs trivial issues — the hook fixes, you review, commit proceeds
B (bugbear) rules catch real bugs: mutable default args, loop variable capture, and friends
pre-commit install wires the git hook once per clone — CI and local now share the same gate
scenes.narration: The workflow after this is installed: you commit, ruff lints and auto-fixes, black normalizes formatting, and only substance reaches review. Add more hooks as the project matures — mypy for type checking, bandit for security scanning, even a hook that regenerates the OpenAPI spec when routes change. The deeper point: every check that CAN be automated SHOULD be, because attention is the scarcest resource on a team and spending it on style is waste. Ruff's speed matters here — a linter that takes milliseconds runs on every commit without friction; one that takes minutes gets bypassed. Design your quality gates to be too cheap to skip.

recap: pytest: plain functions + fixtures (shared, teardown-safe setup) + parametrize (one function, N cases); test contracts, not exact LLM phrasing
Mock at the boundary: FakeProvider records prompts so you assert on inputs (assembly, citations); real-model quality belongs to evals, not unit tests
Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs make production debuggable; ruff + black + pre-commit refuse bad code before review

quiz.q: Why mock the LLM client in unit tests instead of calling the real API?
opts: To save API credits in CI
Real LLM calls are slow, costly, and nondeterministic — the same test could pass and fail with no code change
quiz.why: Determinism is the foundation of testing: mock at the boundary, keep everything your code does testable, and leave model quality to evals.

quiz.q: What does parametrize give you over writing separate test functions?
opts: One function over a data table → N independent test cases in the report, no copied test logic
quiz.why: The test logic lives once; the table is data. Each row reports independently — one failing case never masks another.

quiz.q: What does pre-commit add that CI alone doesn't?
opts: Checks run locally BEFORE commit — bad code never enters history instead of failing after push
quiz.why: The cheapest place to catch an issue is before it exists: shift-left means the same gates run on every developer's machine, every commit.

code.title: The quality loop: tests + fake LLM + structured logging
code.body:
import logging, json, pytest

log = logging.getLogger("rag")

class StructuredFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        return json.dumps({
            "ts": self.formatTime(record),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "event": record.msg if isinstance(record.msg, str) else None,
            **getattr(record, "fields", {}),   # extra context rides along
        })

async def ask(rag, question, request_id):
    log.info("ask.start", extra={"fields": {
        "request_id": request_id, "q": question[:80]}})
    answer = await rag.ask(question)
    log.info("ask.done", extra={"fields": {
        "request_id": request_id, "abstained": answer.abstained}})
    return answer

# In tests: caplog captures everything — assert on LOGGED events:
def test_abstention_is_logged(rag, caplog):
    with caplog.at_level(logging.INFO, logger="rag"):
        asyncio.run(ask(rag, "totally unknown thing?", "req-1"))
    abstentions = [r for r in caplog.records
                   if getattr(r, "abstained", None) is True]
    assert abstentions, "expected an abstention event in the logs"
annot: caplog makes log assertions first-class: 'the system logged an abstention' is a testable behavior
request_id flows into every record → test asserts the correlation field exists, production uses it
The structured formatter keeps one code path for dev (pretty) and prod (JSON) via config

notes:
# Testing & Quality

## pytest
- Plain functions + assert; fixtures injected by name; yield → teardown.
- `@pytest.mark.parametrize` — data-driven cases, independent reports.
- LLM apps: test CONTRACTS (grounded, abstains, validates), not phrasing.

## Mocking LLMs
- Never call real APIs in unit tests: slow, costly, nondeterministic.
- FakeProvider pattern: deterministic replies + records prompts → assert on INPUTS (context assembly, citation rules).
- Model quality → evals (GA-20/21), not unit tests.

## Logging
- Levels: DEBUG/INFO/ERROR; structured JSON; correlation/request IDs.
- Log retrieval telemetry (rewrites, scores, sources) for quality debugging.
- Never log secrets/PII; redact at the boundary.

## Automation
- ruff (lint, fast, --fix) + black (format) + pre-commit (gates on every commit).
- Shift-left: same checks locally and in CI; too cheap to bypass.
